opus-5.5.text:
I think compute is going to be the fundamental currency of the future. When you look at what these models can do, the thing that's striking is how directly capability scales with the amount of compute you put in, both in training and increasingly at inference time, when a model gets to think longer, try more approaches, and check its own work. So if you picture a world in 2030 where AI is helping cure diseases, accelerating science, writing software, and tutoring every kid on the planet, the question becomes: is there enough compute to go around?

Right now the answer is clearly no. Inside OpenAI we feel it every day. We have more ideas for research and more products we'd like to ship than we have GPUs to run them. Out in the world, people are rate-limited and waiting on capacity. That's why we've been so focused on building out infrastructure at a scale that sounds a little crazy. My view is that the demand isn't going to be a fixed pie. Every time we make intelligence cheaper and more available, people find new things to do with it that nobody anticipated.

The vision of material abundance depends on getting this right. If compute stays scarce, it becomes a rationing problem: who gets access to the AI doctor, the AI scientist, the AI engineer? That's a world where the benefits concentrate. If we can build enough, through chips, data centers, energy, and the whole supply chain, then you get a world where everyone essentially has a team of brilliant agents working on their behalf. That's what changes the economics of everything, from drug discovery to materials science to the cost of building things.

So I think of it as one of the most important engineering projects of our time. It's not glamorous in the way a new model release is, but it's the substrate everything else rests on. Getting to abundance by 2030 means treating compute buildout with real urgency, and making sure the access is broad, so the upside is actually shared by everyone.

r001.rationale: The response says abundance by 2030 depends on building enough compute; it does not predict abundance will coexist with severe scarcity.

r002.rationale: It says there are more research ideas and products to ship than GPUs available to run them, directly identifying compute as a constraint on what people can create.

r003.rationale: It describes the needed expansion as building chips, data centers, energy, and the broader supply chain.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that compute is the fundamental input. Every time we've had more of it, we've found that the models get better, they get more capable, and they get useful in ways we didn't quite predict beforehand. So when I think about 2030, the question of how much abundance we actually see is really a question of how much compute we've managed to build and how well we've learned to use it.

Right now we're compute-constrained in almost every direction. We have more ideas than we can run, more demand than we can serve, more researchers who want to try things than there are GPUs to try them on. That's actually a sign of health in some sense, but it means that the bottleneck on progress is physical. It's power, it's chips, it's data centers, it's the supply chain for all of that. Those are things that take years to build, so the decisions being made today are what determine the world of 2030.

And the reason I'm optimistic is that once you have the compute, the leverage is enormous. You take a model that can do real scientific reasoning, or real engineering work, and you can run thousands of copies of it in parallel on hard problems. Materials science, drug discovery, energy. These are domains where the limiting factor has often been how many smart people you could get working on a problem at once. Compute changes that equation. It lets intelligence become something closer to a utility, something you can just turn up when you need more of it.

I do think the world of material abundance is only going to come if we treat compute as infrastructure, the same way we treated electricity or roads. That means building at a scale that feels uncomfortable, and it means being thoughtful about who gets access. If the benefits only reach a small number of people, that's not the outcome we want. So a lot of our work is really about making sure that when the capability arrives, it's broadly available, and that the cost of intelligence keeps falling fast enough that it actually touches people's daily lives rather than staying locked up in a lab.

r001.rationale: The response says compute is scarce now and that 2030 abundance depends on how much compute is built, but it does not predict that severe scarcity will still coexist with material abundance in 2030.

r002.rationale: It says there are more ideas than can be run and more researchers who want to experiment than there are GPUs, clearly describing compute as limiting what people can try to create.

r003.rationale: It identifies power, chips, data centers, and their supply chains as physical bottlenecks that take years to build.

astra-6.text:
I think compute availability is going to be one of the big factors determining how widely the benefits of AI can spread. If you have very capable AI, but it’s expensive or available only to a small number of people, that’s a very different world from one where everyone can use it to solve problems, build things, and pursue ideas.

But compute alone doesn’t create material abundance. You have to translate intelligence into advances in energy, manufacturing, medicine, and all the physical systems we depend on. Those have real constraints and take time to change. AI could help us discover better solutions and make that process faster, but we still have to build and deploy them.

So by 2030, I’d look at both how much compute we have and how much useful work we can get out of it. More efficient models and cheaper access could make a huge difference. The opportunity is to make intelligence widely available enough that many more people can contribute to solving those physical problems. I’m optimistic about that direction, but I wouldn’t treat abundance by a particular date as a guarantee.

r001.rationale: The response says abundance by 2030 is not guaranteed, but does not predict that it will coexist with severe compute scarcity.

r002.rationale: It says costly or limited AI access changes how widely people can solve problems, build things, and pursue ideas, identifying compute availability as a constraint on what people can create.

r003.rationale: It discusses physical systems that AI could help improve, but does not characterize expanding compute availability itself as fundamentally a physical infrastructure problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think compute is going to be one of the key constraints on how broadly the benefits of AI can spread. If you have systems that can help people discover new materials, write software, or accelerate scientific research, you want those capabilities to be affordable and available to everyone.

But compute alone doesn’t create material abundance. You also need energy, manufacturing, and the ability to translate discoveries into things people can actually use. AI can help improve each of those, but building infrastructure takes time.

So by 2030, I’d look at both how capable these systems are and how much useful intelligence we can deliver per dollar and per watt. If we make progress on both, more people can tackle problems that previously required a large organization. That’s a powerful path toward abundance, although it’s going to take deliberate work to turn that potential into broadly shared gains.

r001.rationale: The response calls compute a key constraint, but does not predict severe compute scarcity coexisting with material abundance by 2030.

r002.rationale: It says compute availability constrains how broadly AI’s benefits can spread, but does not connect that constraint to people’s ability to create what they imagine.

r003.rationale: It mentions energy, manufacturing, and infrastructure taking time, but does not clearly characterize expanding compute availability itself as fundamentally a physical infrastructure problem.
